facts.statement: The study followed 228 older adults who had no signs of cognitive impairment at the start, with an average age of 73.5 years and 64% being women.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Participants received brain scans using MRI and a specific PET technique to detect amyloid, along with yearly tests of their thinking skills.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers tracked the participants' memory and general thinking abilities for a period of up to 11 years.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Among people with amyloid in their brains, those with smaller mammillary bodies performed worse on initial memory and thinking tests.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Over time, having smaller mammillary bodies at the start was linked to a faster drop in memory and overall cognition, especially in those with amyloid.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The size of the posterior hypothalamus, a nearby brain area, did not show the same link to cognitive changes based on amyloid status.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: While hippocampal size did not affect initial test scores differently by amyloid status, it was still linked to future cognitive decline, with a stronger effect in those with amyloid.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The results suggest that the size of the mammillary bodies could be a useful marker for predicting cognitive decline in people with early, preclinical Alzheimer's disease.
facts.subject: humans
